topic: How HTTPS keeps your data private
scope_note: Conceptual explanation for non-specialists of what HTTPS (HTTP over TLS) does between a browser and a server: identity check, shared key, encrypted data, and what the padlock does and does not mean. No cryptographic maths, no protocol version detail, no statistics.

facts.statement: Ordinary HTTP sends data as readable text, so it is not hidden from the machines it passes through on the way.

Traffic between a browser and a server crosses many devices that are not either of the two ends, such as Wi-Fi access points and routers, and anyone who controls or taps one of them can copy what passes through.
facts.caveat: Say 'can' read plain traffic: most people on a path never look, the point is that nothing prevents it.

facts.statement: HTTPS is HTTP carried inside an encrypted connection set up with the TLS protocol.
Encryption turns readable data into scrambled data using a key, and only someone holding the right key can turn it back into readable data.
At the start of an HTTPS connection the browser asks the server to identify itself, and the server answers with a certificate.
A certificate states which website name it was issued for and is vouched for by a certificate authority, an organisation that the browser or operating system already trusts.
The browser checks that the certificate matches the site name being visited, that it has not expired, and that it was issued by an authority the browser trusts.
facts.caveat: Browsers perform further checks too; these three are the ones a non-specialist can follow.

facts.statement: If the certificate check fails, the browser warns the user and by default does not continue silently to the site.
facts.caveat: Users can often override the warning; the lesson should say that doing so removes the protection of the identity check.

facts.statement: The browser and the server agree a shared secret key using a key exchange, in which the values sent over the open network are not enough for a watcher to work out the key.
facts.caveat: Keep it to the idea: the key itself is never sent in the open. Do not describe the maths.

facts.statement: Both ends end up with the same key, while a watcher who recorded the whole exchange does not have it.
After the key is agreed, the browser encrypts what it sends, such as a form submission, with that key, and the server decrypts it with the same key.
A watcher on the path who copies the encrypted data sees only scrambled data that is unreadable without the key.
facts.caveat: The watcher can still see that a connection exists and usually which server it goes to, only not the content.

facts.statement: The server's replies are protected the same way, so the protection covers data in both directions.
The padlock in the browser indicates that the connection to the site is encrypted and that the browser accepted the site's certificate for that site name.
facts.caveat: Browser designs for the padlock and warnings differ and change over time.

facts.statement: The padlock does not show that the site's owner is honest, safe or trustworthy, because a site run by a bad actor can also have a valid certificate for its own name.
The padlock does not protect data once it has arrived: the server's owner receives it in readable form and can store or misuse it.
Before entering sensitive data, check that the site name in the address bar is exactly the one you intend and that the browser shows no certificate warning.
facts.caveat: A good habit, not a guarantee; look-alike names are a common trick, so read the name, not just the padlock.

not_claimed: The padlock means the site is safe or trustworthy
HTTPS hides which site you are visiting from everyone on the path
HTTPS protects data after it reaches the server
HTTPS makes your device immune to malware or phishing
Any specific percentage of sites using HTTPS or of attacks, without a source
The key is sent across the network inside the encrypted data in the open
Encryption cannot ever be broken (do not make absolute claims)
